title: UNCERTAIN: f100r plant 8, a spiny flattened pad with the label soity, which Tucker and Talbert read as nashtli (nochtli, prickly pear)
sources: Beinecke MS 408, f100r, canvas 1006248. The drawing and its label: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006248/880,600,340,560/full/0/default.jpg (drawing plus label); the label alone at https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006248/950,1010,200,140/full/0/default.jpg.

ZL 3b locus f100r.8 (pinned data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt) gives soity for this label; the eleven short labels of the upper two registers of f100r are f100r.1..11 and their left-to-right order on the scan was checked directly (f100r.1 chosaroshol, f100r.2 sochorcfhy, f100r.3 otear are the three labels of the top row, left to right).

Arthur O. Tucker and Rexford H. Talbert, 2013, A Preliminary Analysis of the Botany, Zoology, and Mineralogy of the Voynich Manuscript, HerbalGram 100:74-89, https://web.archive.org/web/20150226041323/http://cms.herbalgram.org/herbalgram/issue100/HG100-voynich-online.pdf. p. 76: 'plant No. 8 of the 16 plants on folio 100r; this is obviously a cactus pad or fruit, i.e., Opuntia spp., quite possibly Opuntia ficus-indica (L.) Mill. (Cactaceae)... Thus, [glyph] is quite easily transliterated as nashtli, a variant of nochtli, the Nahuatl (Aztec) name for the fruit of the prickly pear cactus or the cactus itself'. The appendix entry repeats it under Cactaceae (p. 79).

The same article's plant No. 4 on folio 100r is read as maguoey (maguey, Agave atrovirens); its inline glyph image matches the label ZL gives as f100r.4 chofary in shape sequence and in position on the page, which is what fixes their plant numbering to the ZL locus numbers (checked on the same scan: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006248/1330,90,420,200/full/0/default.jpg).
statement: UNCERTAIN; here is what I checked. On the scan, the label ZL transcribes as soity (f100r.8) stands at the lower right of a single drawing: a flattened oval green body, widest above and tapering below into a narrow neck and a reddish-brown taproot, with short stiff projections spaced along both margins and a few wavy hair-like lines on the left edge, and two small dots on the surface. Of the sixteen drawings on the folio this is the one that most reads as a prickly-pear pad, so Tucker and Talbert's 'plant No. 8' and this drawing appear to be the same object. Their numbering is not defined in the article, so I pinned it two ways: their inline glyph image for the No. 4 name maguoey matches the shape and position of the label ZL gives as f100r.4 chofary, and their inline glyph image for nashtli matches the shape sequence of this label (a 2-like s, a loop o, a tall middle glyph, and a final descender), so No. N = f100r.N. What is against it: the projections along the margin are drawn the way this scribe draws leaf teeth elsewhere on the same page, and a flattened pad that narrows into a neck and a taproot is not how Opuntia pads are drawn in the 16th-century Mexican sources Tucker and Talbert compare with; the pale dome ringed by radiating leaflets two drawings to the left (f100r.7) is at least as good a candidate for a bristled fruit. There is one published identification here, not two, and the Nahuatl reading of the label is the authors' own proposal rather than an independent identification of the drawing. Exposure: I read Tucker and Talbert's claims for f100r before looking at the scan, so this is not a blind round; it is a check of whether their claim survives looking, which for the pad it narrowly does.
